transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO, Crowbar), Sofia Martinez (ML Engineer), Evan Chu (Infra Lead)

Auto-summary (auto):
Crowbar is evaluating Redwood to power an internal code-assist and document search feature. Primary decision points are: time-to-first-token for a quicklaunch PLG path vs security/VPC requirements for production. They asked about SOC2, SSO, KMS, and whether Dedicated vs Private on-prem is necessary for initial pilot.

Topics: quickstart credits, time-to-first-token, hosted vs dedicated vs VPC/private, security (SOC2 SAML KMS), benchmarking, batching/latency tradeoffs, rollout strategy.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. We'll do a quick run, get context, and Liam will go through the more technical bits.
[00:10] Raj: Thanks Maya, appreciate it. I'm Raj, CTO at Crowbar. We have Sofia and Evan on as well. We're exploring a path to get a simple code-assist feature out to internal folks first, then expand. Primary questions: can we get to first token fast, and what does production look like from a security and network perspective.
[00:28] Maya: Great, that's exactly what we help with. Quick question—what's your current infra and where would you like to start, hosted or self-hosted?
[00:36] Sofia: Right now we're on GCP for most services, some private repos in GitLab EE, CI on Cloud Build. For proofs we prefer something self-serve but we have regs around data access so we'd likely need VPC peering or Private deployment for the pilot later. For the very first sprint though, we'd like something that just works with minimal setup.
[01:05] Maya: Perfect. Quick-launch path: we provide self-serve API keys and free credits for a trial—time to first token can be minutes if you use our hosted API and our SDK quickstarts. If you need VPC/private we can also do a Redwood Private with a customer-managed control plane, but that typically takes more paperwork.
[01:25] Evan: How much more paperwork? And what do you mean by customer-managed control plane?
[01:33] Liam: (SE) Hi, Evan — Liam. The Private option is where the control plane runs in your VPC or on-prem and we give tooling to orchestrate inference nodes. It requires network config, a Light KMS integration if you want keys on your side, and some onboarding steps—usually a few weeks to a month depending on approvals. Dedicated is middle-ground: reserved GPUs in our cloud with VPC peering options, faster to start.
[02:01] Raj: OK. For ramp 1 we want to avoid long lead times. If hosted can meet our compliance checkboxes, we'd prefer that. What compliance do you have?
[02:09] Maya: We are SOC 2 Type II and have ISO 27001 audit reports available. We also support SAML/SSO, RBAC for tokens, audit logs, and integration with KMS for data-at-rest encryption keys. I'll attach our security packet after the call.
[02:24] Sofia: And data residency — our docs contain internal PII occasionally. We need to make sure logs don't persist beyond X days. Can you configure retention?
[02:33] Liam: Yes, for hosted we provide configurable retention policies and can disable long-term storage for customer prompts. For Dedicated/Private you get full control. Note that what we call 'prefix KV caching' (sometimes transcribed as K-V cash in my notes) can be scoped per-tenant to avoid accidental cross-tenant leakage.
[02:58] Raj: Latency is also a big factor — we want interactive code assist with p95 under 180ms ideally. Is that realistic on hosted?
[03:06] Liam: p95 180ms is challenging for larger LLMs on general workloads. For shorter contexts and smaller models (we can recommend distillation/quantized variants) it's achievable. For strict SLOs you might pick Dedicated pools close to your region or use caching to hit those metrics. We'll share benchmark numbers.
[03:26] Maya: Quick note on credits: we can provide two test credits for the team to run an initial throughput/latency test. That usually answers the time-to-first-token question.
[03:34] Sofia: Awesome. On benchmarking—what's the best way to test inference? Do you have a script or harness?
[03:40] Liam: Yes, we have a lightweight benchmark script that hits the streaming endpoint and measures cold and warm latency, token cost and throughput. I'll share it after the call. For Representative tests send us sample prompts and expected token lengths.
[03:56] Raj: Great. Another question—what about model variants? Can we pin a model version and rollback?
[04:03] Maya: Yes, we offer version pinning and rollout controls (canary, A/B), and automatic fallback to compatible model variants if capacity is constrained. All of that is exposed in the console.
[04:17] Evan: For VPC peering, we'd need details on ports and IPs and whether you open inbound connections. We prefer an egress-only flow.
[04:26] Liam: For hosted we use egress-only outbound webhooks usually; VPC peering and private link options are available for Dedicated/Private. I'll include a network diagram.
[04:34] Sofia: About costs — curious how batching and continuous KV caching reduce cost; can you explain simply?
[04:41] Liam: Sure. Batching groups simultaneous requests to the same GPU which reduces per-token overhead; KV caching stores previous key-value attention states for repeated prefixes so you don't re-send the entire context. Both reduce cost but batching can add a few milliseconds of latency depending on traffic shape. Our Optimize toolkit suggests batch sizes and cache TTLs per workload.
[05:05] Raj: Any limitations with monorepo code contexts — like very long contexts or doc retrieval + folding?
[05:12] Liam: For very long contexts we recommend retrieval+chunking, maybe embeddings + reranking. Also you can use quantized models to reduce cost. We'll help pick models and quantization profiles.
[05:25] Maya: Putting this together: short-term plan could be 1) Hosted quickstart using free credits to validate functionality and latency, 2) Run the benchmark script on your sample prompts, 3) If security checks pass, either go Dedicated with VPC peering or Private if you need full on-prem control.
[05:44] Raj: Sounds good. A couple of practical questions: how long to get an AE/SE-led POC running? And what does the pilot license look like?
[05:53] Maya: For a basic POC on hosted it's usually under a week — you could be calling APIs in hours, but for a wider pilot with SSO and log retention changes expect 1–2 weeks for config and approvals. We'll provide some pilot credits and a short SOW if you want reserved capacity.
[06:12] Sofia: For SSO — do you support multiple identity providers? We use Okta.
[06:16] Liam: Yes, we support SAML-based SSO with Okta, Azure AD, and others. We also have fine-grained RBAC roles.
[06:24] Raj: Any nasty gotchas with log retention and billing data? We need to avoid logs being stored in third-party analytics for certain classes of data.
[06:33] Maya: We can restrict forwarding to third-party analytics and disable ingestion. We'll include specifics in the security packet but it's a standard request and we've handled it for customers with similar constraints.
[06:45] Evan: Network/topology follow-up — do you need us to open inbound ports or will everything be egress?
[06:51] Liam: For hosted, egress is fine. For Dedicated/Private there are options: PrivateLink, VPC peering, or we can run the control plane in your VPC as mentioned. I'll mark this as a follow-up and share a short network doc.
[07:05] Maya: Switching gears — timeline and stakeholders: who else needs to be involved from your side?
[07:11] Raj: Product lead and legal for the pilot SOW. Legal will want the SOC 2 and DPA. Infra (Evan) for network. ML team (Sofia) for prompts and quality checks.
[07:23] Maya: Great — we'll send the security packet and a sample SOW.
[07:28] 
[10:30] (jump forward—note: automatic timestamps every so often, some sections elided)
[10:32] Sofia: A question on model explainability — can you tie responses back to sources in a deterministic way?
[10:39] Liam: We have structured output support and tool-calling patterns that can include provenance metadata. For retrieval-augmented pipelines we can return which doc chunk produced the top candidates. Not strictly deterministic but reproducible under controlled retrieval.
[11:10] Raj: If we do the quickstart, will there be rate limits that impact the test?
[11:15] Maya: We apply soft rate limits on free trials, but we'll bump them for POCs if needed. For production we have quota management and token-level billing.
[12:00] Evan: About rollback and canary — if you push a model that regresses, what's the failure mode? Do you have auto-fallback?
[12:08] Liam: We support automatic fallback to a pinned compatible variant and canary rollouts with traffic shifting. Also integrate with alerting for quality regressions tied to eval prompts.
[12:30] Raj: What's the typical cost delta between hosted and dedicated for steady-state?
[12:36] Maya: Costs vary by throughput and model family. Dedicated gives better per-token economics at scale because you're reserving GPU capacity; hosted is simpler for small scale but can be higher per-token. We'll provide a sample cost model once you share expected QPS and token lengths.
[13:02] Sofia: One more — does Redwood support on-prem GPUs like A100s behind a firewall?
[13:09] Liam: Yes, Private supports on-prem, but that is the heaviest lift: packaged deployment, networking, KMS/HSM integration, plus a bit more ops. We do have partners that handle the on-prem installation if needed.
[13:27] 
[30:15] (near the end)
[30:18] Maya: Ok to recap quickly — action items and next steps: I'll send SOC2 + network diagram and SOW template; Liam will share benchmark script and allocate test credits; Raj will provide traffic profile and SLOs; we tentatively schedule a deeper infra deep-dive next week.
[30:38] Raj: Yep that works. I'd like the deep dive to include concrete latency numbers on our sample prompts.
[30:46] Liam: We'll run the benchmark against a couple of models, both quantized and non-quant, and show cold vs warm p95.
[31:00] Sofia: Also please include a note about prompt log retention and how to turn it off for certain request classes.
[31:06] Maya: Noted.
[31:10] Evan: Last question — competitors: we've looked at Anthropic for chat, and SageMaker endpoints for in-house. How do you compare?
[31:20] Maya: Short answer: Redwood is inference-first with tooling to move from hosted to Dedicated to Private without rewriting code. We focus on observability, rollouts and cost controls. We'll send a short comparison doc but avoid pushing marketing in the transcript.
[31:38] Raj: Cool. Thanks everyone, that's helpful.
[31:42] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the packet.
[31:45] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attributed speaker labels, some technical terms may be rendered phonetically (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache). Recorded at medium quality audio — overlapping talk in a couple of spots.
